Fuck yeah my time to shine, I actually do this a lot. Sadistic_bastard outlined the basics pretty well but I want to flesh out some of the details.

  1. There are several different sizes of caches, ranging from "micros" which are usually the size of a film canister (because they are one), or an Altoids tin, to Large caches that are "bigger than a breadbox and smaller than a house".

  2. The cache will almost always contain a piece of paper for people to sign, kind of like a guestbook. Most people date their signature, as this is kind of half the fun, coming across caches that have been around for years. The paper is usually contained in a little baggy to protect it from water and bugs, but sometimes they aren't or time takes its toll and someone will eventually replace it.

  3. There are several sites and apps to use, but the most popular and in my opinion best is the Geocaching.com site and app. The app is especially nice as it features a live map, so you can see caches that are around you in real time. From there you can select ones you want to find and it will download the exact coordinates the "owner" set for it as well as any information they provided, such a hints, or hazards. This app also lets you "check in" so to speak. You can leave comments saying if you found it or it was missing, or whether it is in good condition or not, as well as leaving a star rating.

  4. Some caches are much easier than others, and some are next to impossible, and some will require you to almost (or completely) break the law to find (mostly just trespassing). I have found caches buried under trees with exposed roots, in magnetic key holders attached to the underside of anything you could possibly imagine (light poles in parking lots are popular), in weird secluded parts of the woods where there is nothing for miles, and right next to objects that a thousand people pass a day. It really is a high tech scavenger hunt and if you like adventure or just finding things it can be a super fun hobby. It does require patience and a hint of finesse if you don't want "muggles" (people who don't geocache) finding the cache and stealing it or getting suspicious of why you're looking under street lights.

  5. The only thing you need is a good GPS. No, your TomTom won't work, but your phone will do just fine. If you want to get super serious you can buy a dedicated GPS that will be even more accurate, but I've been using regular CDMA phones for years without much issue. A phone also doubles as a list and journal so you can track your progress and search for more caches.

  6. Some caches have objects inside. The etiquette is to leave an object if you take one, but you are also free to leave one and take nothing. Most of the time it's little random trinkets like buttons or beads or stuff of very little value. Sometimes it's an object fitted with a GPS tracker, they're usually shaped like cute little bugs and they have writing on them telling you where they originated from or give you instructions on how to track its course. These are designed to be taken and placed in others caches in the hopes that they will travel as far as possible, with the owner usually checking its location every few months. There are stories of bugs traveling through multiple continents and sometimes making it all the way back. One of my favorites was a soldier deployed in Iraq who found one that started somewhere here. If I remember right he brought it back and found the owner. The micros usually only contain a guest list, but that's my favorite part anyway.

  7. You should really try this at least once. Download the app and check the map. Find a micro with a low difficult rating and try it out. I promise there's one within 5 miles of you and if it's fun at all, the harder ones will only be even more fun.

Source: Geocacher for 6 years.

If you like learning the history of things you should look into something called letterboxing. It's not nearly as popular as it used to be but it's basically what led to geocaching. It was the same basic concept but instead of hiding caches, people would hide wooden boxes that contained a unique rubber stamp. Letterboxers would keep a journal of stamps they have collected and many would have their own unique rubber stamper to stamp the letterbox's guest book.
